title: Focus on one metric: why startups should chase 2x-3x moves, not small tweaks
summary: Jason Cohen relays Noah Kagan's advice that a startup can focus on only one metric and should ignore the rest. Using WP Engine, he shows why shaving cancellation rate from 3% to 2.5% pales next to doubling or tripling sign-ups, even if cancellations rise. Small optimizations can wait.

principles.text: A startup can focus on only one metric. Pick it and ignore everything else.
principles.quote: A startup can focus on only one metric. So you have to decide what that is and ignore everything else.

principles.text: A small company has no time for small changes; 10x traffic beats a tiny conversion bump.
principles.quote: At a little company there's no time for small changes achieving small goals. Increasing conversion rates from 0.9% to 1.1% doesn't matter if only 100 people come to the website every day. Much more important is getting 1,000 people to come to the website every day.

principles.text: Optimize the small stuff later. It is mechanical, doable and in your control.
principles.quote: you can always optimize that little stuff later. You can always eke out 0.1% more conversion rate. Or even 1%. Of course you can.

principles.text: Pursue needle-moving levers: doubling revenue, the funding story, viral coefficient above 1, or an active user base.
principles.quote: Focus on the big thing where, if you moved the lever, it would significantly change the business. It doubles revenue or solidifies the funding story or pegs the viral coefficient above 1 or builds the asset of having an active user base.

principles.text: Don't let a secondary metric block growth: tripling sign-ups while cancellations double still nearly triples growth speed.
principles.quote: What if you got sign-ups to triple? And cancellation rate doubled, from 3% to 6%. You'd still be growing almost three times faster.

principles.text: Choosing one metric tells you which actions count as big stuff versus secondary, and breaks you out of incremental changes.
principles.quote: part of this "only do big stuff" means knowing what "big stuff" is, versus the secondary stuff. And to do that, you have to focus on only one metric.
